linguistics.meaning: Purple Haze — ‘our way is hazy / we ride through the haze’ (community translation of the Hendrix-titled trail)

morphemes.gloss: initial: ‘at night, in the dark, dimly’ — the same root in nîpâ‑pimohtêw ‘s/he walks at night’ and nîpâyâstêw ‘the northern lights’
VII conjunct stem: ‘it is bad/ugly/unclear’ — combined with nîpâ‑ to give the sense ‘it is dark/hazy/obscured (like at night)’
AI conjunct, 1pl-incl: ‘when/while we (all of us) pass through, when we go through it’ — verb stem pekise‑ ‘pass through, ride through’ + ‑yâhk first-person plural inclusive conjunct ending

relatedForms.english: Night, at night (the bare temporal form)

morphemes.gloss: VII verb: ‘it is night, it is dark.’ The nîpâ‑ initial in the headword carries the same dim/dark idea but as a productive verb-initial.

relatedForms.note: Free-standing verb for ‘it is night.’ The nîpâ‑ initial in the headword is the bound version of this dim/dark concept.

relatedForms.english: It is bad / it is ugly (VII)

morphemes.gloss: VII verb: ‘it is bad, ugly, unpleasant, hard to see clearly.’ Inside the headword this stem is what nîpâ‑ modifies.

relatedForms.note: ‘It is bad/unclear.’ With the night-initial nîpâ‑ it produces ‘it is hazy / it is bad-as-at-night’ — the visibility-blurring sense the trail name plays on.

morphemes.gloss: AI verb stem: ‘to pass through, to make one’s way through, to ride/walk through’

relatedForms.note: The independent (3sg) form. The plaque uses the conjunct 1pl-incl pekiseyâhk ‘when we (all) ride through.’

quickReference.english: Purple Haze (community translation of the Hendrix title)
quickReference.note: Headword on the plaque. Two-word phrase: VII (impersonal ‘it is dim/hazy’) + AI conjunct (‘when we ride through it’).

quickReference.english: It is night / it is dark
quickReference.note: The free-standing ‘night’ verb that the nîpâ‑ initial echoes.

quickReference.english: It is hazy / unclear / hard to see
quickReference.note: The first word of the plaque, treated as a stand-alone VII.

quickReference.english: When we (all of us) pass through it
quickReference.note: AI conjunct, 1pl-incl. ‑yâhk is the inclusive ‘we including you’ ending.

There is no single ‘purple’ root in Plains Cree; common formations use sîpihko‑ ‘blue’ + a colour-shading final, or borrow from the wider colour vocabulary. The plaque deliberately does NOT translate the colour word but renders the IDEA — ‘the haze we ride through.’

baseWords.english: (initial) at night, in the dark, dimly

culturalStory.heading: About nîpâmâyâtân pekiseyâhk — the Haze We Ride Through
body: Purple Haze is a Hendrix song before it is a trail, and the trail name is itself a borrow — when the local builders carved the Cree, they did not try to translate the colour ‘purple’ literally (which Plains Cree does not have a single root for) but instead rendered the FEELING of the song and the trail: the dim, hazy way of moving through. The plaque on the wall is unusually pictorial for the set: a two-tone purple mountain silhouette under a pink-fading-to-violet sky, the syllabics ᓂᐹᒫᔮᑖᐣ ᐯᑭᓭᔮᕽ in clean white above the mountain, ‘PURPLE HAZE’ in white block letters across the violet base.

The Cree breaks into two parts. nîpâmâyâtân is a VII (it-verb): nîpâ‑ ‘in the dark, at night, dimly’ + ‑mâyâtan ‘it is bad / ugly / unclear,’ together meaning roughly ‘it is hazy / dim / hard to see’ (the sense Hendrix gets at with ‘purple haze all in my eyes’). pekiseyâhk is an AI conjunct in the first-person-plural inclusive: ‘when we (all of us) pass through it.’ Read together: ‘when it is hazy and we (all) pass through it’ — the rider’s phrase, not a colour name.

The trail itself is in the Hawrelak/Central Edmonton (North) network, neighbour to Wonder Woman, Lovers Lane, and Victoria’s Secret in the river-valley clusters under ᓀᐦᐃᔭᐤ ᐊᐢᑭᕀ Nêhiyaw‑Askiy (Plains Cree territory). On the wall there are two Purple Haze plaques — a small portrait-format one in row 1 (the one wired here) and a fuller one further right — both reading the same Cree.

notes: PHYSICAL SIGN OVERRIDES CATALOGUE: The plaque is carved with SRO 'nîpâmâyâtân pekiseyâhk' (with circumflex on the first î; final ‑hk on pekiseyâhk). The current catalogue creeName 'nipâmâyâtan pekisehyânik' is materially different — it is missing the î circumflex on the first vowel, missing the n-final on ‑mâyâtân, has a spurious ‑hy‑ in pekise(h)yâhk, and ends in ‑ânik instead of ‑yâhk. Coordinator should update catalogue creeName to 'nîpâmâyâtân pekiseyâhk'.

PHYSICAL SIGN OVERRIDES CATALOGUE (syllabics): Catalogue creeSyllabics 'ᓂᐹᒫᔭᑕᐣ ᐯᑭᓭᐦᔮᓂᐠ' encodes the broken catalogue SRO. The plaque-correct syllabics for nîpâmâyâtân pekiseyâhk is 'ᓂᐹᒫᔮᑖᐣ ᐯᑭᓭᔮᕽ'. Coordinator should update creeSyllabics accordingly.

The first-vowel diacritic on nîpâ‑ is read with MEDIUM confidence from the small upper plaque crop (a clear circumflex is visible on the first 'i'). Some local materials write 'nipâ‑' without the î; both are attested. The carving here uses î.

Morpheme analysis nîpâ‑ + ‑mâyâtan + pekise‑ + ‑yâhk is the structural reading. nîpâ‑ + ‑mâyâtan as a single VII is established (in itwêwina the headword nîpâmâyâtan ‘it is dim/hazy/dusk’ exists). The conjunct pekiseyâhk is a 1pl-inclusive form of the AI verb pekise‑ ‘pass through’. This morpheme breakdown carries ~75% confidence; an alternative reading parses pekiseyâhk as a different stem (pîkise‑ ‘break/disperse’). Suggest user review by an elder or itwêwina cross-check.

The trail name is a community translation of the Hendrix song title; it is NOT a literal colour translation. Plains Cree does not have a single ‘purple’ root (formations use sîpihko‑ ‘blue’ + colour-shading finals).
